description: Genetic and environmental variation, natural selection, fossil evidence for evolution, speciation.
content_html:
Variation Within a Species

Individuals within a species are not identical — they show variation. Some variation is genetic (arising from differences in alleles, such as blood type), some is environmental (caused by living conditions, such as a scar or language spoken), and much is a combination of both (height depends on genes but also on diet). Genetic variation arises through three main routes: mutations (random changes in DNA sequence), meiosis (the shuffling and random assortment of chromosomes during gamete formation), and sexual reproduction (combining alleles from two different parents).

Variation within a population is essential for natural selection. Without variation, all individuals would respond identically to environmental pressures — selection would have nothing to act upon. It is variation that makes evolution possible.

Key Fact

Variation can be genetic, environmental or both. Genetic variation comes from mutations, meiosis and sexual reproduction. Without variation, natural selection cannot occur.

Natural Selection and Evolution

Natural selection was proposed by Charles Darwin (1809–1882) and, independently, by Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913). Their joint theory was presented to the Linnean Society in 1858. The theory works through four linked steps:

1. Within a population, individuals show variation in their characteristics.
2. More offspring are produced than the environment can support, so individuals compete for limited resources (food, water, mates, space).
3. Those with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce — survival of the fittest.
4. Survivors pass the advantageous alleles to their offspring, so over many generations the proportion of individuals with the beneficial trait increases.

This cumulative change across generations is evolution. It is crucial to remember that individual organisms do not evolve — populations evolve as the frequency of advantageous alleles changes over time. Evolution has no direction or purpose; it simply reflects which traits happen to be best suited to the current environment.

Antibiotic resistance is a modern, observable example of natural selection. When a population of bacteria is exposed to an antibiotic, most individuals die. However, random mutations may have given some bacteria a resistance mechanism. These resistant individuals survive, reproduce rapidly (bacteria can divide every 20 minutes) and pass on the resistance allele. Over time, the resistant strain comes to dominate the population.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a well-known example. To slow the spread of resistance, antibiotics should only be prescribed when necessary, patients must complete the full course, and overuse in agriculture should be minimised. New antibiotics are difficult to develop, so preserving the effectiveness of existing ones is critical.

Key Fact

Natural selection: variation → competition → survival and reproduction of the fittest → advantageous alleles inherited by offspring. Repeated over many generations, this drives evolution.

Evidence for Evolution

Evidence for evolution comes from several independent sources:

• The fossil record — fossils show gradual changes in organisms over millions of years, including transitional forms linking ancient and modern species. Fossils can be dated by the rock layers in which they are found (older strata lie deeper), by radiometric dating techniques, and by comparison with other fossils of known age. Gaps in the fossil record exist because fossilisation is rare, but new discoveries continue to fill these gaps.
• Comparative anatomy — different vertebrate species share similar underlying bone structures (the pentadactyl limb: five-digit structure found in human hands, bat wings and whale flippers), suggesting common ancestry despite very different functions.
• DNA analysis — closely related species share more DNA sequences. The more similar the DNA, the more recently the species diverged from a common ancestor. Molecular evidence now allows evolutionary trees to be constructed with great precision.

The peppered moth provides a well-documented example of natural selection within observable timescales. Before industrialisation, pale-coloured moths were better camouflaged on pale, lichen-covered tree bark; dark moths were eaten more often by birds. As industrial pollution darkened tree trunks with soot and killed lichens, dark moths gained a survival advantage. The proportion of dark moths increased substantially in industrial areas. When clean air legislation reduced pollution, the pale form recovered. This demonstrates that natural selection responds rapidly to environmental change.

Speciation occurs when populations of the same species become isolated — most commonly through a geographical barrier such as a mountain range, sea channel or river. Once isolated, the two populations face different environments and different selection pressures. Random mutations and natural selection cause each population to change in different directions over many generations. Eventually, the populations become so genetically different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. At this point, they are classified as separate species.

Extinction occurs when a species cannot adapt fast enough to changing conditions. Causes include climate change, new predators or competitors, new diseases, habitat destruction and catastrophic events. The fossil record shows that the vast majority of species that have ever lived are now extinct. Current extinction rates are elevated compared to the geological average, linked to human activity including habitat destruction, pollution and climate change.

Key Fact

Speciation: geographical isolation → different selection pressures → populations evolve separately → reproductive isolation → two distinct species. Evidence for evolution comes from fossils, comparative anatomy and DNA analysis.
exam_tip_html: For a ‘3 marks — Explain’ question on natural selection, use the four-step structure: variation, competition, survival of the fittest, inheritance of advantageous alleles. Apply it specifically to the organism named in the question — a generic description loses marks. For antibiotic resistance questions, make clear that the resistant bacteria were not ‘created’ by the antibiotic; resistance arose from a random mutation that already existed before exposure. The antibiotic selected for it, not caused it. For speciation questions, always include geographical isolation, different selection pressures, and reproductive isolation as three distinct steps.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Variation arises from mutations, meiosis and sexual reproduction. It is essential for natural selection: variation → competition → survival and reproduction of the fittest → alleles inherited by offspring → population change over generations.
  • Antibiotic resistance is natural selection in bacteria: random mutations give resistance; the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce. Overuse of antibiotics accelerates this process.
  • Evidence for evolution includes fossils (gradual change over time), comparative anatomy (shared bone structures indicating common ancestry) and DNA analysis. Speciation occurs when geographically isolated populations diverge until they can no longer interbreed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a source of genetic variation in a population?
A) Mutations in DNA
B) Meiosis shuffling chromosomes
C) Sexual reproduction combining alleles from two parents
D) Mitosis producing genetically identical cells
practice_questions.marks: D) Mitosis producing genetically identical cells [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of evidence scientists use to support the theory of evolution.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two from: fossil record / comparative anatomy / DNA analysis / observed examples (e.g. antibiotic resistance, peppered moth) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how geographical isolation can lead to speciation.
practice_questions.marks: A geographical barrier separates a population into two isolated groups [1 mark]; each group evolves separately under different selection pressures until they become so different they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in a population of bacteria. Use the concept of natural selection in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Random mutations give some bacteria resistance to the antibiotic [1 mark]; when the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria survive and reproduce while non-resistant bacteria are killed [1 mark]; resistant bacteria pass on the resistance allele to offspring, so over time the resistant strain becomes dominant in the population [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A scientist studies a population of dark-coloured and pale-coloured moths living in a woodland. After a period of heavy air pollution that darkened the tree trunks, she records that the proportion of dark moths has increased significantly.
Explain these observations using the theory of natural selection.
practice_questions.marks: Before pollution, pale moths were better camouflaged on pale tree trunks, so dark moths were more visible to predators and eaten more often [1 mark]; after pollution darkened the tree trunks, dark moths became better camouflaged and more likely to survive and reproduce [1 mark]; dark moths passed on the alleles for dark colouring to offspring, so the proportion of dark moths in the population increased over generations [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the evidence for the theory of evolution by natural selection, considering both supporting evidence and historical challenges to the theory's acceptance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed evaluation of at least three types of evidence with specific examples; addresses historical resistance with reasoned explanation; reaches a justified conclusion about strength of evidence.
Secure: Clear explanation of two or more evidence types with examples; some discussion of historical context; conclusion present.
Developing: One or two types of evidence described without full evaluation; limited historical context.
Emerging: Simple list of evidence types without explanation.

Points may include:
Supporting evidence: fossil record shows gradual change; comparative anatomy (pentadactyl limb); DNA analysis shows degree of relatedness; observable examples within human timescales (antibiotic resistance, peppered moth).
Historical challenges: contradicted prevailing religious explanations for creation; insufficient fossil record at the time (gaps now largely filled); genetics not yet understood in Darwin's era (Mendel's work on heredity was not linked to Darwin's theory until the modern synthesis of the 20th century).
Conclusion should weigh strength of evidence.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes natural selection?
options: Organisms deliberately adapt to suit their environment
Organisms with advantageous characteristics survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles
All organisms in a population compete equally for resources

knowledge_checks.q: What must happen first for speciation to occur?
Genetic variation in a population arises from mutations, meiosis and _____.
The fossil record, comparative _____ and DNA analysis are three types of evidence for evolution.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: Survival and reproduction of best-adapted individuals
Gradual change in inherited characteristics of a population
Formation of a new species through reproductive isolation

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three sources of genetic variation in a population?
In what year did Darwin and Wallace present their joint theory of natural selection?
What is the first step of natural selection?
flashcard_questions.a: Individuals in a population show variation in their characteristics.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do individuals within a population compete?
flashcard_questions.a: Resources (food, water, mates, space) are limited and there are more offspring than can survive.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to advantageous alleles after natural selection?
flashcard_questions.a: They are passed to offspring, increasing in frequency across generations.

flashcard_questions.q: What is antibiotic resistance an example of?
flashcard_questions.a: Natural selection — resistant bacteria survive antibiotic treatment and pass on resistance.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two types of fossil evidence that support evolution.
flashcard_questions.a: Fossils showing gradual change in form; transitional fossils linking ancient and modern species.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the pentadactyl limb and what does it suggest?
flashcard_questions.a: A five-digit limb structure shared by many vertebrates, suggesting common ancestry.

flashcard_questions.q: How does geographical isolation lead to speciation?
flashcard_questions.a: Isolated populations evolve separately until they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The permanent disappearance of a species when no living individuals remain.

glossary_terms.definition: Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species, caused by genetic differences, environmental differences, or a combination of both.
The process by which organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment survive, reproduce and pass on their advantageous alleles, changing the characteristics of a population over time.
The gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations, driven by natural selection.
The ability of bacteria to survive exposure to antibiotics that would previously have killed them, resulting from natural selection favouring resistant mutations.

The formation of a new species when populations of the same species become so genetically different, usually through geographical isolation, that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The permanent disappearance of a species when no living individuals remain, caused by failure to adapt to environmental change, new predators, disease or catastrophic events.
